{{< include _poly-kit.qmd >}}

Jazz rhythm sits on a steady four, but a great deal of it plays *against* that four. The tension is part of
its West African inheritance through the blues and New Orleans music.

## Swing: three inside two

A swung eighth note is close to a triplet: the beat is felt in three while the bass walks in four and the
music is counted in two-beat halves. The ride cymbal pattern "ding, ding-a ding" sits on triplets:

<div class="poly" data-layers="X..X.x;2" data-names="Ride (triplets);Two beats" data-sounds="bell;kick" data-bpm="70" data-beat="1"></div>

Swing ratios vary with tempo and player; the even triplet here is a starting point only.

## Three-beat figures across the bar

A common jazz device is a phrase that repeats every three eighth notes (or every dotted quarter) over 4/4.
It goes round the bar, landing on a different beat each time, and meets the downbeat again after three bars.
This is polymeter: same pulse, different lengths.

<div class="poly" data-layers="X..;X.x.x.x." data-names="Dotted-quarter figure;4/4 (eighths)" data-sounds="hi;kick" data-bpm="100" data-beat="1" data-polymeter></div>

Pianists use it in comping and solos; horn sections in big band riffs.

## 3 against 4 and 4 against 3

Drummers and pianists also play true even polyrhythms over the beat, such as three half-note triplets
across a 4/4 bar or quarter-note triplets (three against two beats).

<div class="poly" data-layers="4;3" data-names="Four beats;Half-note triplets" data-sounds="kick;hi" data-bpm="80" data-beat="0"></div>

<div class="poly" data-layers="2;3" data-names="Two beats;Quarter-note triplets" data-sounds="kick;hi" data-bpm="80" data-beat="0"></div>

## Players to hear

Drummers known for playing across the time include Elvin Jones (with John Coltrane's quartet), Max Roach,
Tony Williams and Jack DeJohnette; pianists include McCoy Tyner and Brad Mehldau. This list is from memory and
is a starting point for listening, not a checked claim about particular recordings.

## Practice

1. Keep the four with your foot. Clap the dotted-quarter figure until you can stop on any downbeat without losing it.
2. Mute the figure in the player and play it on your instrument over the four.
3. Play quarter-note triplets for one bar, then back to quarter notes, without the beat moving.

The skill is to keep the time *steady* while the figure crosses it: if the four moves to follow the figure,
the effect is gone.
